title: User-defined data types
overview: Topic 13.1 is about data types that the programmer writes into the program, rather than ones the language supplies. You need to explain why they are needed, then define and use the two non-composite kinds (enumerated and pointer) and the three composite kinds (record, set and class/object) in Cambridge pseudocode: TYPE Name = (value1, value2) for an enumeration, TYPE Name = ^INTEGER for a pointer, TYPE Name ... ENDTYPE for a record, TYPE Name = SET OF CHAR with DEFINE for a set, and CLASS ... ENDCLASS for a class. Paper 3 and Paper 4 questions usually give a scenario and ask you to write the type declarations, to use them (dot notation, dereferencing with ^), or to choose and justify the most suitable type. Marks come from exact syntax and from reasons tied to the data in the scenario.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of why user-defined types are necessary.
Define and use non-composite types, including enumerated and pointer.
Define and use composite data types, including set, record and class/object.
Choose and design an appropriate user-defined data type for a given problem.

definitions.definition: A type supplied by the programming language, such as INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN or DATE, for which the language already fixes the range of values and the operations allowed.
A data type whose definition the programmer writes in the program (with TYPE in pseudocode); variables can then be declared with it like any built-in type.
A data type that can be defined without referencing another data type and contains only one data type; it can be primitive (INTEGER, BOOLEAN) or user-defined (enumerated, pointer).
A collection of data items, of different (or the same) data types, grouped under a single identifier; it can be user-defined (record, set, class) or built in (array, string).
A non-composite user-defined type whose definition lists every value a variable of that type may take; the values are ordered.
A non-composite user-defined type used to reference a memory location: its variables store an address, and the definition indicates the type of data stored at that address.
Following a pointer to reach the value stored at the address it holds, written PointerName^ in Cambridge pseudocode.
A composite user-defined type made of a fixed number of named fields, which may have different data types, declared with TYPE ... ENDTYPE.
A composite type holding an unordered collection of values of one data type, with no duplicates and no index, on which set operations such as membership, union and intersection can be carried out.
A composite user-defined type that combines attributes (data) with the methods that act on them; it is the blueprint from which objects are created.
An instance of a class, created in pseudocode with NEW, holding its own values for the class attributes.

sections.title: Built-in types, user-defined types and why they are needed
content: Built-in types (INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE) have values and operations fixed by the language. A user-defined type is constructed by the programmer, with TYPE in pseudocode, and can then be used in DECLARE statements like any built-in type.

They are needed because real problems involve data the language designer could not predict: an order that can only be at one of four stages, or a book with a title, a price and a loan status. Defining the type extends the flexibility of the language, keeps related data under one identifier and restricts variables to valid values.

Every type is either composite or non-composite. A composite type is a collection of several data items, of different (or the same) data types, grouped under a single identifier; its definition refers to other data types. A non-composite type can be defined without referencing another data type and holds a single value; it can be a primitive (built-in) type or a user-defined one. Do not confuse user-defined types with abstract data types such as stacks, which are defined by their operations.
bullets: Purpose: to create a new data type that is not available in the language (it extends the flexibility of the language).
User-defined types are constructed by the programmer, not supplied by the language.
They model the problem's data, make code easier to read and allow only valid values.
Composite: multiple elements, of different or the same data types, grouped under a single identifier; its definition refers to other data types. Examples: record, set, class/object.
Composite types can be user-defined (record, class) or built in (array, string).
Non-composite: defined without referencing another data type; contains only one data type. Examples: any primitive type, enumerated, pointer.
Non-composite types can be primitive (INTEGER, BOOLEAN) or user-defined (enumerated, pointer).

examples.label: Classifying the user-defined types in this topic
examples.content:
Type        | Category      | Pseudocode definition
Enumerated  | non-composite | TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered)
Pointer     | non-composite | TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL
Record      | composite     | TYPE TBook ... ENDTYPE (fields declared inside)
Set         | composite     | TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE
Class       | composite     | CLASS Ticket ... ENDCLASS

Test: does the definition group several items of other types under one name? Yes = composite.
A pointer mentions a type (^REAL) but still holds just one value, an address, so it is non-composite.

sections.title: Enumerated types
content: An enumerated type is defined by listing every value a variable of the type can take: TYPE <identifier> = (value1, value2, ...). The values are identifiers, not strings, so they are written without quotes. Because they form an ordered list, they can be compared with < and >, and adding 1 gives the next value (check for the last value first).
bullets: Enumerated type: a non-composite type with an ordered list of all possible values.
Syntax: TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered).
Declare: DECLARE Stage : TStage. Assign: Stage ← Packed (no quotes).
Values are ordinal: Stage >= Dispatched and Stage + 1 are valid.
Benefits: readable code; only the listed values can be stored; comparisons follow the list order.

examples.label: Tracking an online order with an enumerated type
examples.content:
TYPE TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered)

DECLARE Stage : TStage

Stage ← Packed
IF Stage < Delivered THEN
   Stage ← Stage + 1               // move on to the next stage
ENDIF
IF Stage >= Dispatched THEN
   OUTPUT "Your parcel is on its way"
ELSE
   OUTPUT "Your parcel is still in the warehouse"
ENDIF

examples.label: Trace of the order-stage code
examples.content:
Position of each value: Placed 1, Packed 2, Dispatched 3, Delivered 4

Statement                  | Stage       | Notes
Stage ← Packed            | Packed      | position 2
Stage < Delivered?         |             | 2 < 4, TRUE
Stage ← Stage + 1         | Dispatched  | position 3
Stage >= Dispatched?       |             | 3 >= 3, TRUE
Output: Your parcel is on its way

Had Stage been a STRING, the comparison "Dispatched" >= "Packed" would compare letters
(D comes before P), giving FALSE: alphabetical order is not the order of the stages.
(Checked with a Python IntEnum: Stage(Packed + 1) is Dispatched.)

sections.title: Records
content: A record type groups a fixed number of named fields, which can have different data types, under one identifier. It is defined with TYPE Name, one DECLARE line per field, and ENDTYPE. Fields are reached with dot notation, and an array of records holds a table whose columns have different types, keeping each item's data together when sorting or searching. Python has no record type, so a class or dataclass is used instead.
bullets: Record: composite; a fixed number of named fields, possibly of different data types.
TYPE TBook ... DECLARE Field : Type ... ENDTYPE.
Field access with dot notation: ThisBook.Title, Library[Index].OnLoan.
A field can be of another user-defined type (e.g. an enumerated type) or an array.
Whole records can be assigned in one statement: Copy ← Library[2].
An array of records replaces parallel arrays and keeps each item's fields together.

examples.label: A book record containing an enumerated field, used in an array
examples.content:
TYPE TGenre = (Fiction, History, Science)

TYPE TBook
   DECLARE Title : STRING
   DECLARE Price : REAL
   DECLARE OnLoan : BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Genre : TGenre
ENDTYPE

DECLARE Library : ARRAY[1:5] OF TBook
DECLARE Index, LoanCount : INTEGER
DECLARE LoanValue : REAL

Library[1].Title ← "Tide Maps"
Library[1].Price ← 12.50
Library[1].OnLoan ← TRUE
Library[1].Genre ← Fiction
// ... books 2 to 5 set up in the same way

LoanCount ← 0
LoanValue ← 0.0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
   IF Library[Index].OnLoan = TRUE THEN
      LoanCount ← LoanCount + 1
      LoanValue ← LoanValue + Library[Index].Price
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT LoanCount, " books on loan, worth ", LoanValue

examples.label: Trace: counting books on loan
examples.content:
Index | Title           | Price | OnLoan | Genre   | LoanCount | LoanValue
      |                 |       |        |         | 0         | 0.00
1     | Tide Maps       | 12.50 | TRUE   | Fiction | 1         | 12.50
2     | Quiet Engines   | 8.99  | FALSE  | Science | 1         | 12.50
3     | Salt Roads      | 15.00 | TRUE   | History | 2         | 27.50
4     | Glass Harbour   | 9.75  | FALSE  | Fiction | 2         | 27.50
5     | Small Moons     | 11.20 | TRUE   | Science | 3         | 38.70

Output: 3 books on loan, worth 38.7
(Recalculated with a Python list of records: 3 on loan, total 38.70.)

sections.title: Classes and objects as user-defined types
content: A class is a composite user-defined type that holds attributes (data) and the methods that act on them. Attributes are normally PRIVATE and reached only through PUBLIC methods (encapsulation). In pseudocode: CLASS Name ... ENDCLASS, a constructor PROCEDURE NEW, and ObjectName ← NEW ClassName(parameters). Inheritance and polymorphism belong to 20.1.
bullets: Class = attributes + methods; record = fields only.
Object = an instance of a class, created with NEW.
PRIVATE attributes are accessed through PUBLIC methods (encapsulation).

examples.label: A class holding a ticket's data and the method that uses it
examples.content:
CLASS Ticket
   PRIVATE Band : STRING
   PRIVATE BasePrice : REAL

   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenBand : STRING, GivenPrice : REAL)
      Band ← GivenBand
      BasePrice ← GivenPrice
   ENDPROCEDURE

   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetPrice() RETURNS REAL
      IF Band = "VIP" THEN
         RETURN BasePrice * 2
      ELSE
         RETURN BasePrice
      ENDIF
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS

DECLARE MyTicket : Ticket
MyTicket ← NEW Ticket("VIP", 18.50)
OUTPUT MyTicket.GetPrice()        // 18.50 * 2 = 37.0

sections.title: Pointer types and dereferencing
content: A pointer variable stores the memory address of another data item, not the data itself. The pointer type names the type of data found at that address: TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL. A variable of that type is declared without a caret.

^Price (caret before) means 'the address of Price'. PricePtr^ (caret after) means 'the value at the address held in PricePtr' (dereferencing); assigning to PricePtr^ changes Price itself. Use the 2026 guide's ^ form, not the coursebook's @. The guide defines no null value; a question will say what to use.
Pointers let dynamic data structures (linked lists, trees) grow and shrink at run time. Python has no pointer type; it handles references automatically.
bullets: Pointer type: non-composite; used to reference a memory location.
It stores an address, and its definition indicates the type of data stored at that address.
Define: TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL. Declare: DECLARE PricePtr : TRealPointer (no caret).
Address of a variable: ^Price. Dereference: PricePtr^.
Changing PricePtr^ changes the variable pointed to.
Used to build dynamic structures (linked lists, trees) that change size at run time.

examples.label: Reading and changing a value through a pointer
examples.content:
TYPE TRealPointer = ^REAL

DECLARE PricePtr : TRealPointer
DECLARE Price, Discounted : REAL

Price ← 40.0
PricePtr ← ^Price                  // PricePtr now holds the address of Price
Discounted ← PricePtr^ * 0.75      // dereference: 40.0 * 0.75
PricePtr^ ← 52.0                   // writes 52.0 into Price
OUTPUT Discounted, " ", Price

examples.label: Memory view of the pointer example (addresses invented for illustration)
examples.content:
Address | Identifier | After line 3 | After line 4 | After line 6
3012    | Price      | 40.0         | 40.0         | 52.0
3020    | Discounted | ?            | ?            | 30.0
3028    | PricePtr   | ?            | 3012         | 3012

Line 5: PricePtr^ looks in address 3012 and finds 40.0; 40.0 * 0.75 = 30.0.
Line 6: PricePtr^ ← 52.0 writes into address 3012, so Price becomes 52.0.
Output: 30.0 52.0
PricePtr itself never changes from 3012.
(Checked with a Python ctypes pointer: dereferenced value * 0.75 = 30.0, then the target reads 52.0.)

sections.title: Set types
content: A set holds values of one data type with no order, no index and no duplicates. The guide defines it in two steps: TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE Chess ("Ana", "Ben") : TNameSet. Set operations (membership, union, intersection, difference) have no keywords in the 2026 guide, so describe them in words or use the notation a question gives.
bullets: Set: composite; unordered values of one type, no index, no duplicates.
TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, then DEFINE SetName (values) : TNameSet.
Operations: membership, add, remove, union, intersection, difference.
Loading values into a set removes duplicates automatically.
No operator syntax in the 2026 guide: describe set operations in words.

examples.label: Defining two sets (guide syntax only)
Set operations on the two clubs

sections.title: User-defined types in a real language
content: Paper 4 uses a real language. In Python an enumeration comes from the enum module (IntEnum keeps values ordered), a record is a class or dataclass, a set is built in, and there is no pointer type because every variable already holds a reference.
bullets: Enumerated: class Stage(IntEnum) in Python; Enum in Java and VB.NET.
Record: dataclass or class in Python; Structure in VB.NET; class in Java.
Set: built-in set in Python; HashSet in Java and VB.NET.
Pointer: no pointer syntax in Python or Java; references are automatic.

examples.label: Python versions of the enumerated, record and set examples
examples.content:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import IntEnum


class Stage(IntEnum):          # enumerated type: every value listed, in order
    PLACED = 1
    PACKED = 2
    DISPATCHED = 3
    DELIVERED = 4


@dataclass
class Book:                    # record type: named fields of different types
    isbn: str
    title: str
    price: float
    on_loan: bool


stage = Stage.PACKED
stage = Stage(stage + 1)       # ordinal: the next value in the list
assert stage is Stage.DISPATCHED and stage >= Stage.DISPATCHED

shelf = [
    Book("978-0001", "Tide Maps", 12.50, True),
    Book("978-0002", "Quiet Engines", 8.99, False),
    Book("978-0003", "Salt Roads", 15.00, True),
]
on_loan = sum(1 for book in shelf if book.on_loan)
assert on_loan == 2

chess = {"Ana", "Ben", "Chen", "Dev", "Eli"}      # set type: no order, no duplicates
robotics = {"Chen", "Eli", "Farah", "Gus"}
assert chess & robotics == {"Chen", "Eli"}         # intersection
assert len(chess | robotics) == 7                  # union
assert chess - robotics == {"Ana", "Ben", "Dev"}   # difference
assert "Gus" in robotics                           # membership
assert set(["Ben", "Ana", "Ben", "Chen"]) == {"Ana", "Ben", "Chen"}

sections.title: Choosing and designing a user-defined type for a problem
content: Match each part of the scenario's data to a type and justify the match with a feature of that data. Then write the full declaration: define enumerated and set types before the record that uses them, and give every field a suitable data type (an ID with leading zeros is a STRING, a yes/no fact is BOOLEAN).
bullets: Fixed list of named values: enumerated.
Several related values of different types about one thing: record (array of records for many).
Membership only, no duplicates, no order: set.
Data plus the operations on it, with protected attributes: class.
Links between items, size changing at run time: pointer.

comparisonTable.title: The five user-defined types compared
rows: A value must come from a short, fixed list of named options
A memory address of a REAL
Items must be linked or the structure must grow at run time
One value per named field; fields can differ in type
One item is described by several facts of different types
TYPE TNameSet = SET OF STRING, DEFINE ...
Unordered values of one type, no duplicates
Only membership matters and repeats must be excluded
Data needs its own operations and protection (OOP)

diagram.title: Choosing a user-defined type from the data
nodes: Read what the scenario says about the data
One of a fixed list of named values? Use an enumerated type
Several facts of different types about one item? Use a record (array of records for many items)
Only membership matters, no duplicates? Use a set
Data plus its own operations? Use a class
Items linked, size changes at run time? Use pointers
Write the TYPE declarations, defining enumerations and sets before the record that uses them

analysisChains.title: Why an enumerated type beats a STRING for an order status
steps: An order status is stored as a STRING and a clerk types "Dispatchd"
The STRING variable accepts the misspelling, and later tests for "Dispatched" silently fail
Declared as TStage = (Placed, Packed, Dispatched, Delivered), the variable can hold only the four listed values, so the typo is rejected
Because the values are ordered, Stage >= Dispatched finds every order that has left the warehouse in one comparison
analysisChains.evaluation: The enumerated type prevents invalid values and gives a meaningful order; a STRING would compare alphabetically (Dispatched before Packed), which is not the order of the stages.

analysisChains.title: Array of records versus parallel arrays
steps: A library keeps titles, prices and loan flags in three separate arrays matched by index
Sorting by price must swap the same positions in all three arrays; missing one swap attaches a title to the wrong price
With DECLARE Library : ARRAY[1:5] OF TBook, one swap of Library[J] and Library[J + 1] moves every field of the book together
A 2D array cannot replace them because its elements must all share one type, and the fields are STRING, REAL and BOOLEAN
analysisChains.evaluation: A record type keeps each item's data together and allows mixed field types, so an array of records is the safer design whenever each item has several facts.

analysisChains.title: Why pointers allow dynamic data structures
steps: A program must store an unknown number of customers, possibly a few, possibly thousands
With a fixed array the programmer must guess a large upper bound, wasting memory, and the program fails if the guess is exceeded
With a pointer type, each new item can be stored wherever memory is free and linked in by storing its address in the previous item
The structure grows one item at a time and shrinks when items are removed, with no upper bound declared in advance
analysisChains.evaluation: Pointers trade simple indexing for flexibility: the structure uses only the memory it needs, but items can only be reached by following addresses, not by jumping to an index.

examTips: Copy the Cambridge syntax exactly: TYPE Name = (value1, value2); TYPE Name = ^Type; TYPE Name ... ENDTYPE with a DECLARE per field; TYPE Name = SET OF Type with DEFINE. A missing ENDTYPE or field data type loses the mark.
For 'why are user-defined types needed' give two points: to create a new data type not available in the language (extends its flexibility), and so the programmer can model the data the problem needs.

To define composite, say 'multiple data items, of different or the same types, grouped under a single identifier' plus an example; for non-composite, say 'defined without referencing another data type' plus an example.
Enumerated: say 'an ordered list of all possible values'. Pointer: say 'stores the address of a memory location and indicates the type of data stored there'. 'Stores data' earns nothing.
When choosing a type, give the type and a reason from the scenario, e.g. 'record, because each student has an ID, a name and a date of birth of different data types'.
For pointers keep the three forms apart: ^Type in the TYPE line, ^Variable for 'address of', Pointer^ for the value pointed to.
commonMistakes: Putting enumerated values in quotation marks, as if they were strings.
Writing the caret in the variable declaration (DECLARE P : ^TRealPointer); the caret belongs only in the TYPE definition.
Saying a pointer stores the data item; it stores the address of the item, and PricePtr^ is needed to reach the value.
Describing a record as an array: array elements all share one type and are reached by index, while record fields have names and can differ in type.
Inventing set-operation keywords as if they were official; the 2026 guide defines only TYPE ... SET OF and DEFINE.
Calling a set composite because it 'holds many values' but then giving it an index; a set has no order and no positions.
Confusing user-defined types with abstract data types: a stack is defined by its operations, whatever types are used to build it.

quickRecall.question: Why are user-defined data types necessary?
quickRecall.answer: The built-in types cannot model the specific values or groups of fields a problem needs, and the language cannot know them in advance, so the programmer defines them; this improves readability and restricts data to valid values.

quickRecall.question: Name the two non-composite and three composite user-defined types.
quickRecall.answer: Non-composite: enumerated and pointer. Composite: record, set and class/object.

quickRecall.question: Write a Cambridge definition of an enumerated type for the stages of a traffic-light sequence: Red, RedAmber, Green, Amber.
What does 'ordinal' mean for an enumerated type?
quickRecall.answer: The values have an order given by the definition, so they can be compared and the next value found.

quickRecall.question: Given TYPE TIntPointer = ^INTEGER, DECLARE P : TIntPointer and a variable Count, how do you make P point to Count and then output Count's value through P?
Give two differences between a record and an array.
quickRecall.answer: Record fields can have different data types, array elements share one type; record fields are reached by name with dot notation, array elements by index.

quickRecall.question: State three properties of a set.
quickRecall.answer: Its values have no order, it has no index, and it contains no duplicates (all values are of one type).

quickRecall.question: How does a class differ from a record?
quickRecall.answer: A class holds methods as well as data, and its attributes are usually private, reached only through its methods; a record holds only fields.

quickRecall.question: Which type would you choose for a list of permitted file extensions that is only ever checked for membership?
quickRecall.answer: A set, because only membership matters, order is irrelevant and duplicates must not appear.
